practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — The Living World

questions.question: Binomial nomenclature was introduced by
questions.explanation: Linnaeus — Species Plantarum (plants) and Systema Naturae (animals). Each name has two components: generic and specific epithet.

questions.question: In Mangifera indica, the word 'indica' denotes the
questions.explanation: indica = specific epithet (species), Mangifera = genus. Both are Latinised and printed in italics.

questions.question: The correct ascending sequence of taxonomic categories is
options: Species → Genus → Order → Family → Class → Phylum → Kingdom
Genus → Species → Family → Class → Order → Phylum → Kingdom
Species → Genus → Family → Order → Class → Phylum → Kingdom
Species → Order → Family → Class → Genus → Kingdom → Phylum
questions.explanation: Kingdom (least inclusive to most inclusive upward): species, genus, family, order, class, phylum/division, kingdom. Learn it as K-P-C-O-F-G-S upward.

questions.question: A herbarium sheet carries
options: a dried, pressed and preserved plant specimen with a label
questions.explanation: Herbaria are the storehouses of dried, pressed, preserved specimens mounted on sheets along with a label of date, place and collector.

questions.question: The number of species described so far is about
questions.explanation: Roughly 1.7–1.8 million species are known against an estimated total of 7 million. The number keeps rising as new species are discovered.

questions.question: Taxonomic keys are analytical aids that use
options: contrasting characters arranged as couplets in pairs
the complete list of synonyms of a species
questions.explanation: Each couplet has two statements with contrasting characters; choosing one (lead) leads to the next couplet. Keys are of separate types for plants, animals and even families.

questions.question: A species is best defined as
options: any group of organisms living in one habitat
a group of individuals with fundamental similarities able to interbreed
questions.explanation: Fundamental similarities plus the ability to interbreed define a species. Mango, wheat and Homo sapiens are all single species.

questions.question: Museum specimens are preserved in
options: formalin or alcohol and as dried/pinned specimens
questions.explanation: Museums keep collections of preserved plant and animal specimens, along with skeletons, insect boxes and taxidermied animals.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — The Living World

questions.question: A monograph contains information on
options: all the plants of a city
questions.explanation: A monograph gives detailed information on any one taxon — the complete study of a single group, unlike a flora which covers a region.

questions.question: A flora contains
options: the index to the plant species found in a particular area
the life history of one species
the key to animal phyla only
questions.explanation: Flora, manuals, monographs and catalogues are all means of recording descriptions and help in correct identification.

questions.question: The term 'taxon' represents
options: a taxonomic group of any rank
questions.explanation: Insecta is a taxon at class level, Mammalia likewise — a taxon is a real group of organisms, while a category is its rank.

questions.question: ICBN stands for
questions.explanation: ICBN gives the rules of plant nomenclature; animals follow ICZN. Both rules come from international congresses and the system was started by Linnaeus.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a taxonomic aid?
questions.explanation: Herbaria, botanical gardens, museums, zoos, keys, flora, manuals, monographs and catalogues are the taxonomic aids; nitrogen-fixing root nodules are a plant structure.

questions.question: Herbarium sheets are arranged according to
options: a universally accepted system of classification
questions.explanation: A universally accepted system of classification keeps herbaria usable across the world — this is why herbaria serve as a quick referral system.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Biological Classification

questions.question: The five-kingdom classification was proposed by
questions.explanation: Whittaker (1969) used cell structure, thallus organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. Woese later added the domain system.

questions.question: Archaebacteria differ from other bacteria mainly in
options: having a different cell wall structure that helps them survive extreme habitats
questions.explanation: Their cell walls are built differently, which is why they survive halophilic, thermoacidophilic and methanogen habitats — hence the name 'ancient' bacteria.

questions.question: Which of these is a dinoflagellate responsible for red tides?
questions.explanation: Gonyaulax multiplies so rapidly that the sea appears red, and it releases toxins that kill fish. Dinoflagellates have two flagella.

questions.question: Diatoms are characterised by
options: a siliceous cell wall with two overlapping halves (like a soap box)
questions.explanation: Diatoms' indestructible silica walls accumulate as 'diatomaceous earth', used in polishing and filtration. They are the chief producers of the oceans.

questions.question: Which fungal class is called 'fungi imperfecti' because no sexual stage is known?
questions.explanation: Deuteromycetes reproduce only asexually by conidia. Many antibiotics and the fungus that causes ringworm belong here.

questions.question: The sexual cycle of fungi involves
options: plasmogamy, karyogamy and meiosis in the zygote
questions.explanation: Fusion of protoplasm (plasmogamy) → fusion of nuclei (karyogamy) → meiosis in the zygote. The result is a haploid spore.

questions.question: Viroids are
options: free DNA with a protein coat
free RNA of very low molecular weight without a protein coat
questions.explanation: Discovered by T. O. Diener in potato spindle tuber disease — the RNA is free, unlike viruses which are nucleoprotein particles.

questions.question: Lichens are a symbiosis between
questions.explanation: The algal component (phycobiont) makes food; the fungal component (mycobiont) provides shelter and absorbs water and minerals. Lichens are pollution indicators.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Biological Classification

questions.question: Which of the following has cell walls made of cellulose?
questions.explanation: Chrysophytes (diatoms and desmids) have cellulosic cell walls, unlike fungal chitin and bacterial peptidoglycan. Mycoplasma has NO cell wall at all.

questions.question: The smallest living cells known and the only ones without a cell wall are
questions.explanation: Mycoplasma are the smallest living cells; they survive without a wall, which is why they are pleomorphic and resistant to penicillin.

questions.question: Cyanobacteria are
options: photosynthetic autotrophic prokaryotes, some fixing nitrogen
questions.explanation: Blue-green algae have chlorophyll a, are often colonial in mucilaginous sheaths, and heterocysts in some fix atmospheric nitrogen (e.g. Nostoc, Anabaena).

questions.question: The fungal classes differ mainly in
options: the mode of spore formation and the type of fruiting body
questions.explanation: NCERT's basis of classification for fungi: mycelium type, mode of spore formation and the fruiting bodies. Cell walls are chitinous in all of them.

questions.question: Which one is a single-celled eukaryotic organism without a cell wall?
questions.explanation: Euglenoids such as Euglena have a protein-rich pellicle instead of a wall; they photosynthesise in light and behave as heterotrophs in its absence.

questions.question: Slime moulds are characterised by
options: saprophytic plasmodium and spores with true walls
questions.explanation: Under suitable conditions they form a plasmodium; at unfavourable times the plasmodium fruits to form spores with true walls — hence the old name 'fungus animals'.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Plant Kingdom

questions.question: The common pigments of Chlorophyceae are
options: chlorophyll a and d and phycoerythrin
questions.explanation: Chlorophyceae (green algae) have chl a and b — same as land plants — and store food as starch. Examples: Chlamydomonas, Volvox, Ulothrix.

questions.question: Agar is obtained from
questions.explanation: Agar, used in ice-creams, jellies and to grow microbes, comes from red algae. Algin comes from brown algae and carrageen from red algae.

questions.question: Bryophytes are called amphibians of the plant kingdom because
options: they grow in both fresh and marine water
they live in soil but need water for sexual reproduction
questions.explanation: Their motile antherozoids need a water film to swim to the archegonium — so they are terrestrial but water-dependent for reproduction.

questions.question: The first group of plants to have vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) is
questions.explanation: Pteridophytes are the first true vascular plants; their well-developed vascular tissue also made them the first with a dominant sporophyte.

questions.question: Heterospory is characteristic of
questions.explanation: Heterospory (two kinds of spores) is the first step towards the seed habit — it appears in some pteridophytes before true seeds exist.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE for gymnosperms?
options: Ovules are enclosed in an ovary
Ovules are not enclosed in an ovary and there is no double fertilisation
questions.explanation: Naked ovules and no fruit — that is the literal meaning of gymnosperm. Endosperm here is haploid and formed before fertilisation.

questions.question: The stored food of brown algae (Phaeophyceae) is
questions.explanation: Pigments: chl a, c + fucoxanthin; food: laminarin/mannitol. Examples are Laminaria, Sargassum, Fucus, Ectocarpus.

questions.question: The largest and economically most important group of plants is
questions.explanation: Flowering plants dominate the present-day vegetation; the smallest is Wolffia (about 0.1 cm) and Eucalyptus is among the tallest.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Plant Kingdom

questions.question: Which one has chlorophyll a, chlorophyll d and phycoerythrin?
questions.explanation: Red algae get their colour from phycoerythrin, store floridean starch, and include Polysiphonia, Porphyra and Gracilaria.

questions.question: A multicellular gametophyte attached to the parent sporophyte is a feature of
options: angiosperms and gymnosperms (retention of the female gametophyte)
questions.explanation: The retention of the female gametophyte (with the egg) on the parent sporophyte is the prelude to the seed habit — a key evolutionary step.

questions.question: In haplontic life cycles the dominant phase is
options: haploid gametophyte with only the zygote diploid
questions.explanation: Example: Volvox, Spirogyra, most algae. Diplontic = dominant diploid sporophyte (angiosperms, gymnosperms); haplo-diplontic = both multicellular (bryophytes, pteridophytes).

questions.question: Which pteridophyte is a heterosporous aquatic fern?
questions.explanation: Salvinia is heterosporous and aquatic. Selaginella is also heterosporous; Pteris and Equisetum (horsetails) are homosporous.

questions.question: Coralloid roots with nitrogen-fixing cyanobacteria occur in
questions.explanation: Cycas bears coralloid roots with Anabaena as an endosymbiont. Cycas also has the largest ovule? No — it is simply a well-known gymnosperm with these roots.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT an economic product of algae?
questions.explanation: Cyclosporin comes from a fungus (Trichoderma polysporum). Agar, carrageen and algin are algal products; Porphyra, Laminaria and Sargassum are used as food.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Animal Kingdom

questions.question: Radial symmetry is found in
questions.explanation: Radial symmetry suits stationary or slow-moving animals; bilateral symmetry appears in animals that move in one direction. Echinoderm larvae are bilateral, adults radial.

questions.question: Which of the following is a diploblastic animal?
questions.explanation: Diploblastic = ectoderm + endoderm with mesoglea in between (Cnidaria, Ctenophora). Tripoblastic animals have a third layer, the mesoderm.

questions.question: Pseudocoelomate animals are
questions.explanation: In pseudocoelomates the body cavity is not lined by mesoderm (Aschelminthes). Platyhelminthes are acoelomate; annelids onward are true coelomates.

questions.question: The water vascular system is a characteristic of
questions.explanation: Used for locomotion, food capture and respiration. Also note their calcareous endoskeleton and tube feet — examples: Asterias, Echinus, Antedon.

questions.question: Malpighian tubules are the excretory organs of
questions.explanation: Arthropods: chitinous exoskeleton, jointed appendages, Malpighian tubules for excretion — the largest phylum of the animal kingdom.

questions.question: Which phylum shows metameric segmentation?
questions.explanation: Metamerism (true segmentation with segments bearing similar organs) appears in annelids. Arthropods also show segmentation but with a different basic plan.

questions.question: Flame cells (protonephridia) for excretion occur in
questions.explanation: Flame cells help in osmoregulation and excretion in flatworms, which are also acoelomate, triploblastic, bilaterally symmetrical and mostly parasitic.

questions.question: A notochord is present in
questions.explanation: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord, paired pharyngeal gill slits and a post-anal tail — the four fundamental chordate characters (Hemichordata has only one of them).

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Animal Kingdom

questions.question: Which of the following is an exclusively marine phylum?
questions.explanation: Echinoderms are all marine; they also have a unique water vascular system and radial symmetry as adults.

questions.question: Cnidarians are characterised by
questions.explanation: Nematocysts on the tentacles are defensive or used to capture prey; polyp and medusa are the two body forms (Obelia shows both).

questions.question: Which character is NOT found in Aves?
questions.explanation: Birds have feathers, pneumatic bones, a four-chambered heart and are warm-blooded, but they lack mammary glands and have no urinary bladder.

questions.question: The phylum with the largest number of species is
questions.explanation: Arthropods make up over two-thirds of all known animal species: insects, spiders, crabs, prawns, centipedes, etc.

questions.question: Which one of the following is a cartilaginous fish?
questions.explanation: Chondrichthyes (Scoliodon, Pristis, Carcharodon) have a cartilaginous endoskeleton and ventral mouth without an air bladder; Exocoetus, Labeo and Hippocampus are bony fishes.

questions.question: Salamander, frog and toad belong to
questions.explanation: Amphibians: moist skin without scales, three-chambered heart, external fertilisation in most, and they need water for reproduction.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Morphology of Flowering Plants

questions.question: Pneumatophores are found in
questions.explanation: Mangrove roots grow vertically upwards for gaseous exchange. Other examples: prop roots of banyan, stilt roots of sugarcane, tuberous roots of sweet potato.

questions.question: Axile placentation is found in
questions.explanation: Axile: ovules on the central axis of a multilocular ovary (tomato, lemon, China rose). Marginal = pea; free central = Dianthus; parietal = mustard; basal = sunflower.

questions.question: Vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation occurs in
questions.explanation: Vexillary is the pea family's characteristic (one big standard, two wings, two keel petals). Valvate = Calotropis; twisted = cotton/lady's finger; imbricate = Cassia/Gulmohar.

questions.question: In Fabaceae the fruit is a
questions.explanation: Legume (pod) — one-chambered, develops from a superior monocarpellary ovary, splitting into two halves. Floral formula: % ⚘ K(5) C1+2+(2) A(9)+1 G1.

questions.question: Diadelphous stamens, marginal placentation and a legume fruit indicate the family
questions.explanation: Fabaceae: stamens 10 in diadelphous condition (9+1), marginal placentation, root nodules with Rhizobium. Pulses, soybean, groundnut, indigofera are all here.

questions.question: Epipetalous stamens characterise
questions.explanation: In Solanaceae the stamens are attached to the corolla (epipetalous), with axile placentation, a berry or capsule fruit — tomato, brinjal, chilli, potato, tobacco, belladonna.

questions.question: The correct sequence of parts in a floral formula (K C A G) refers to
questions.explanation: K = calyx, C = corolla, A = androecium, G = gynoecium; G with a line above indicates an inferior ovary — a notation the exam expects you to read.

questions.question: Racemose inflorescence is characterised by
options: basipetal arrangement with a definite terminal flower
acropetal arrangement with the main axis continuing to grow
questions.explanation: In racemose the youngest flower is at the apex (main axis grows indefinitely); cymose has the oldest at the apex because the main axis ends in a flower.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Morphology of Flowering Plants

questions.question: Which one is a modified stem?
questions.explanation: Potato is a stem tuber (has eyes = axillary buds), while sweet potato, carrot and radish are modified roots — the presence of nodes/buds decides the answer.

questions.question: The fleshy, edible part of the mango fruit develops from the
questions.explanation: Mango is a drupe: epicarp (skin), mesocarp (fleshy edible), endocarp (stony). In coconut the endosperm is edible.

questions.question: In marginal placentation the ovules are arranged
options: in a single row along the ventral suture
at the base of the ovary
questions.explanation: Marginal placentation occurs in a monocarpellary, unilocular ovary — pea is the standard example.

questions.question: Which of the following is a monocot family among the three studied?
questions.explanation: Liliaceae: trimerous flowers, superior ovary, capsule fruit, axile placentation — e.g. Allium (onion, garlic), Colchicum, Tulipa, Aloe.

questions.question: The standard fruit of the mustard family is
questions.explanation: Siliqua (from a bicarpellary syncarpous ovary with parietal placentation) — split by a false septum into two chambers.

questions.question: Rhizome, corm and bulb are examples of
questions.explanation: All three are stems (they bear nodes, buds and scaly leaves): rhizome = ginger/turmeric, corm = colocasia, bulb = onion/garlic.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Anatomy of Flowering Plants

questions.question: Which of the following is a dead tissue?
questions.explanation: Sclerenchyma cells are dead and have thick lignified walls, providing mechanical strength. Parenchyma and collenchyma are living.

questions.question: Casparian strips are found in the
questions.explanation: Suberised Casparian thickenings in the endodermal cells prevent the passage of water and solutes through the cell walls — they must pass through the protoplasm.

questions.question: In a dicot stem the vascular bundles are
questions.explanation: Open = cambium present = secondary growth possible. Monocot stems have conjoint, collateral, closed and scattered bundles — that is why monocots lack secondary growth.

questions.question: Isobilateral (monocot) leaves show
options: stomata only on the lower surface
stomata on both surfaces with bulliform cells
questions.explanation: Monocot leaves are isobilateral with equally distributed stomata and large empty bulliform cells that roll the leaf to reduce water loss.

questions.question: Periderm consists of
questions.explanation: Cork cambium (phellogen) forms cork (phellem, dead, suberised) outward and secondary cortex (phelloderm) inward. Together = periderm, which replaces the epidermis.

questions.question: Which element of phloem is dead at maturity?
questions.explanation: Only phloem fibres are dead; sieve tubes, companion cells and phloem parenchyma are living. In xylem, tracheids and vessels are the dead conducting elements.

questions.question: Annual rings in a dicot stem are formed due to
options: the activity of cork cambium only
the activity of the vascular cambium, with spring wood and autumn wood
questions.explanation: Spring/early wood is lighter and wider, autumn/late wood darker and denser: one pair forms one annual ring, an age record of the tree.

questions.question: The hypodermis of a monocot stem is made of
questions.explanation: Monocot stem hypodermis is sclerenchymatous (dicot stem hypodermis is collenchymatous) — a standard distinguishing point.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Anatomy of Flowering Plants

questions.question: Which of the following tissues is NOT a part of the ground tissue system?
questions.explanation: Ground tissue = everything except epidermis and vascular tissue: cortex, pith and medullary rays.

questions.question: Radial vascular bundles are characteristic of
questions.explanation: In roots the xylem and phloem lie on different radii (alternate), unlike stems where they lie on the same radius (conjoint).

questions.question: The tissue responsible for bending of a young dicot stem without breaking is
questions.explanation: Collenchyma provides mechanical support with flexibility, and its cells are living with cellulose-thickened corners — typical of the hypodermis of dicot stems.

questions.question: Which structure is absent in a monocot root?
questions.explanation: Monocot roots have no vascular cambium, hence no secondary growth; they do have endodermis, casparian strips and a well-developed pith.

questions.question: The function of medullary rays (secondary xylem rays) is
options: conduction of water and food radially and storage
questions.explanation: Rays connect the primary xylem with the primary phloem radially, serving conduction and storage across the secondary growth.

questions.question: Heartwood differs from sapwood in being
questions.explanation: Sapwood is the outer living, conducting region; heartwood is inner, dark, deposited with gums and resins — durable but no longer conducts water.

questions.question: The tissue that lines the inner surface of the small intestine is
questions.explanation: Columnar epithelium with microvilli covers the intestine and helps in absorption. Squamous lines the alveoli and blood vessels; cuboidal lines ducts and tubules.

questions.question: Tendon and ligament are respectively
options: dense regular connective tissue connecting muscle to bone and bone to bone
questions.explanation: Tendons are strong and inflexible (muscle→bone); ligaments are elastic with little matrix (bone→bone) — the difference that keeps joints stable.

questions.question: Cockroach has how many pairs of spiracles?
questions.explanation: Ten pairs of spiracles open into the tracheal system; the 10th pair lies on the 8th abdominal segment. Tracheae divide into tracheoles through which gaseous exchange occurs.

questions.question: The number of chambers in the cockroach heart is
questions.explanation: The cockroach has a 13-chambered heart (dorsal vessel) with haemolymph, an open circulatory system and colourless blood plasma.

questions.question: Excretion in cockroach occurs through
questions.explanation: Malpighian tubules absorb nitrogenous wastes from haemolymph and pour them into the hindgut, from where the faeces are expelled.

questions.question: Which of the following is found only in a male cockroach?
questions.explanation: Males have a pair of anal styles (absent in females); both sexes have anal cerci, compound eyes, antennae and wings.

questions.question: The tissue that stores fat and acts as an insulator is
questions.explanation: Adipose tissue is a loose connective tissue with fat-storing cells, found beneath the skin and between internal organs.

questions.question: Neurons, the structural and functional units of nervous tissue, are
options: excitable cells that generate and transmit nerve impulses
questions.explanation: Neurons are excitable; neuroglia (supporting cells) make up the rest of the nervous tissue, which is the most integrated tissue type.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Structural Organisation in Animals

questions.question: Which one is a fluid connective tissue?
questions.explanation: Blood has a fluid matrix (plasma) with cells and proteins — the only fluid connective tissue, along with lymph.

questions.question: Mouth parts of a cockroach are of
questions.explanation: Cockroach mouthparts: labrum, mandibles, maxillae, labium and hypopharynx — a biting and chewing type suited to an omnivorous diet.

questions.question: The glandular epithelium is made of
options: cuboidal or columnar cells specialised for secretion
questions.explanation: Glandular epithelium forms endocrine (hormone-secreting) and exocrine (enzyme/mucus-secreting) glands.

questions.question: Which cell junction allows rapid transfer of ions between adjacent cells?
questions.explanation: Gap junctions connect the cytoplasm of neighbouring cells for rapid communication; tight junctions prevent leakage, adhering junctions cement cells together.

questions.question: In cockroach, the gizzard (proventriculus) has
options: an inner lining of cuticle with six chitinous teeth to grind food
questions.explanation: The gizzard grinds the food fine; the mouth opens into the pharynx, then oesophagus → crop (storage) → gizzard (grinding) → ileum with hepatic caeca.

questions.question: Which of the following statements is correct about cartilage?
options: It is a solid, flexible connective tissue with chondrocytes in a matrix
It is a type of muscle
questions.explanation: Cartilage is a solid but flexible connective tissue: chondrocytes sit in lacunae within a matrix of chondroitin sulphate, found at joints, the nose, larynx and trachea. It has no blood vessels of its own.

questions.question: Cell theory was extended by Rudolf Virchow with the statement
options: All plants are made of cells
questions.explanation: Virchow (1855) explained that cells arise from pre-existing cells, completing the theory of Schleiden and Schwann.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT found in a prokaryotic cell?
questions.explanation: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, ER, Golgi, plastids) and a true nucleus; they do have 70S ribosomes and a naked DNA.

questions.question: Mesosomes in bacteria are
options: infoldings of the plasma membrane that increase surface area
questions.explanation: Mesosomes are plasma membrane infoldings (also holding the respiratory enzymes), functionally similar to mitochondria in eukaryotes.

questions.question: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed by
questions.explanation: Singer & Nicolson (1972): a lipid bilayer with proteins floating in it, giving quasi-fluid mobility — the accepted model today.

questions.question: The 'powerhouse' of the cell with cristae that increase surface area is
questions.explanation: Mitochondria: double membrane, inner one folded into cristae bearing oxysomes/ATP synthase — they also have their own DNA and 70S ribosomes.

questions.question: Which organelle is known as the suicidal bag of the cell?
questions.explanation: Lysosomes are single-membrane vesicles from the Golgi, full of hydrolytic enzymes that digest anything they engulf — including the cell itself in apoptosis.

questions.question: The site of protein synthesis in a cell is
questions.explanation: Ribosomes are ribonucleoprotein granules, not surrounded by any membrane. Eukaryotic 80S and prokaryotic 70S ribosomes both have two subunits.

questions.question: Chlorophyll pigments in the chloroplast are located in
options: the thylakoid membranes of the grana
questions.explanation: Grana (stacks of thylakoids) hold the pigments for the light reaction; the stroma holds the enzymes for carbon fixation.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Cell: The Unit of Life

questions.question: Which organelle is the site of lipid synthesis and detoxification?
questions.explanation: SER lacks ribosomes and makes lipids/steroids; RER with ribosomes makes proteins — a classic one-line distinction.

questions.question: The nuclear envelope is
options: a double membrane with pores continuous with the ER
questions.explanation: The nuclear envelope bears pores that allow RNA and proteins to move, and the outer membrane is continuous with the rough ER.

questions.question: Chromosomes in a eukaryotic cell consist of
questions.explanation: Chromatin is DNA + histones; at metaphase it condenses into chromosomes with two chromatids joined at the centromere. Some chromosomes also carry satellites.

questions.question: The 9+2 arrangement of microtubules is found in
questions.explanation: Eukaryotic flagella and cilia show 9 peripheral doublets + 2 central (axoneme). Centrioles show 9 triplets — a well-known NEET distinction.

questions.question: Golgi apparatus is principally involved in
options: packaging of proteins and membrane biogenesis
questions.explanation: The Golgi (dictyosomes in plants) modifies and packs proteins and lipids into vesicles — it is the cell's post office.

questions.question: Which of the following is a non-membrane-bound organelle?
questions.explanation: Ribosomes, along with centrioles, are without membranes. All the others are membrane-bound organelles.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Biomolecules

questions.question: The building blocks of proteins are
options: amino acids joined by peptide bonds
fatty acids joined by ester bonds
questions.explanation: Amino acids link by peptide bonds to form polypeptides. A protein is a polymer of about 20 different amino acids.

questions.question: Which one is an essential amino acid in humans?
questions.explanation: Essential amino acids cannot be synthesised in the body and must come from the diet — a favourite NCERT one-liner set.

questions.question: Ribosome, collagen and RuBisCO are all
questions.explanation: RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the biosphere, collagen the most abundant protein in animals — NCERT's two 'most abundant' facts.

questions.question: The secondary structure of a protein refers to
options: local folding of the chain into helix or sheet
questions.explanation: Secondary = α-helix/β-pleated sheet, held by hydrogen bonds. Tertiary = overall 3-D form; quaternary = multiple subunits (e.g. haemoglobin, insulin).

questions.question: Chitin, a polysaccharide, is found in
options: the exoskeleton of arthropods and fungal cell walls
questions.explanation: Chitin is a homopolysaccharide of N-acetylglucosamine — structural in fungi and arthropods. Cellulose (plants) and glycogen (animals) are its cousins.

questions.question: Enzymes are mostly
options: proteins that catalyse biochemical reactions by lowering activation energy
questions.explanation: Some nucleic acids also act as enzymes (ribozymes), but the vast majority are proteins — highly specific, affected by temperature and pH.

questions.question: Which of the following is a competitive inhibitor?
options: A poison binding at an allosteric site
Heavy metal ions denaturing the enzyme
questions.explanation: Competitive inhibitors resemble the substrate and bind the active site (malonate vs succinate). Non-competitive inhibitors bind elsewhere and change the enzyme's shape.

questions.question: NAD and FAD are examples of
questions.explanation: Coenzymes are organic cofactors loosely attached to the apoenzyme; prosthetic groups (like haem) are tightly bound. Metal ions such as Zn²⁺ are the third type.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Biomolecules

questions.question: The six classes of enzymes include
options: oxidoreductases, transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases, ligases
questions.explanation: Every enzyme name ends with -ase, and its class tells you the type of reaction: transferase moves a group, hydrolase adds water, ligase joins two molecules.

questions.question: On a graph of reaction rate against temperature, the curve
options: rises to an optimum then falls sharply as the enzyme denatures
questions.explanation: Optimum temperature is usually 37 °C for human enzymes; above it the tertiary structure breaks and the enzyme is denatured (rate collapses).

questions.question: Which bond links two monosaccharides?
questions.explanation: A glycosidic bond forms with the loss of a water molecule — a condensation reaction. Sucrose, lactose and maltose are disaccharides built this way.

questions.question: Phosphodiester bonds are found in
questions.explanation: In DNA and RNA, the phosphate links the 3'-OH of one sugar to the 5'-OH of the next — this backbone gives the strand its direction.

questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary metabolite?
questions.explanation: Secondary metabolites (alkaloids, terpenes, essential oils, rubber, gums) are not needed for growth or reproduction but have ecological and economic value.

questions.question: Prosthetic group differs from a coenzyme in that it is
questions.explanation: Haem in haemoglobin is a classic prosthetic group; NAD/FAD are coenzymes. Both are organic cofactors.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Cell Cycle and Cell Division

questions.question: DNA replication occurs during
questions.explanation: In S phase the DNA content doubles (2C → 4C) while the chromosome number stays the same. G1 and G2 are growth phases.

questions.question: Chromosomes become visible and identify as two chromatids in
questions.explanation: In prophase, chromatin condenses, centrioles move apart, and the nucleolus and nuclear envelope break down — the classic beginning of mitosis.

questions.question: During anaphase of mitosis
options: centromeres split and sister chromatids move to opposite poles
questions.explanation: Anaphase is the shortest stage: centromeres split and chromatids (now chromosomes) move poleward — the chromosome number temporarily doubles.

questions.question: Cytokinesis in a plant cell occurs by
options: cleavage furrow starting at the periphery
cell plate formation starting at the centre
questions.explanation: A cell plate forms from the centre outward and becomes the middle lamella; in animal cells a cleavage furrow pinches the cell inward.

questions.question: Synapsis of homologous chromosomes takes place during
questions.explanation: In zygotene the homologous chromosomes pair to form bivalents, with the synaptonemal complex developing between them.

questions.question: Crossing over occurs during
questions.explanation: Recombination nodules appear on the synaptonemal complex in pachytene and the enzyme recombinase mediates the exchange of segments.

questions.question: Chiasmata become visible during
questions.explanation: At diplotene the synaptonemal complex dissolves and the homologues pull apart, remaining joined at the chiasmata — the sites of crossing over.

questions.question: The number of chromosomes is reduced to half during
questions.explanation: Meiosis I is the reductional division: homologous chromosomes separate so each daughter cell gets one of each pair.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Cell Cycle and Cell Division

questions.question: Terminalisation of chiasmata occurs in
questions.explanation: In diakinesis chiasmata shift towards the ends of the chromosomes (terminalisation), the spindle is assembled, and the nucleolus disappears.

questions.question: A cell with 2n = 24 undergoing meiosis will produce gametes with
questions.explanation: Meiosis halves the chromosome number: 24 → 12 in each gamete, and gametes get one member of each homologous pair.

questions.question: Which of the following occurs in metaphase I of meiosis but not in mitotic metaphase?
questions.explanation: In metaphase I the paired homologues (bivalents) line up; in mitosis single chromosomes line up. This is why meiosis I is reductional.

questions.question: Sister chromatids separate during
questions.explanation: Anaphase I separates homologues; anaphase II separates sister chromatids — meiosis II is essentially a mitotic division.

questions.question: Meiosis in a diploid cell produces
questions.explanation: One round of DNA replication followed by two nuclear divisions gives four genetically different haploid cells — the basis of gametogenesis.

questions.question: Which phase is the longest in the human cell cycle (24 h)?
questions.explanation: Interphase takes about 23 of the 24 hours; mitosis lasts under an hour. DNA is duplicated in S (~8 h).

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Photosynthesis in Higher Plants

questions.question: The reaction centre pigment of photosystem II is
questions.explanation: PS II = P680 and PS I = P700, both chlorophyll a molecules. Accessory pigments (chl b, xanthophylls, carotenoids) only transfer energy to them.

questions.question: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from
options: the splitting of water at PS II
questions.explanation: Photolysis of water (Hill reaction) provides electrons, protons and O2 — proved by Ruben and Kamen using 18O-labelled water.

questions.question: The light reaction of photosynthesis takes place in
options: the thylakoid membranes of the chloroplast
questions.explanation: Light reaction in thylakoids (photochemical phase) and dark reaction in the stroma (biosynthetic phase) — structure follows function.

questions.question: The first stable product of the Calvin cycle is
questions.explanation: RuBisCO fixes CO2 onto RuBP, immediately giving two molecules of 3-PGA (a 3-carbon compound) — hence C3 plants.

questions.question: The primary CO2 acceptor in C4 plants is
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells fixes CO2 (higher affinity than RuBisCO, no photorespiration) forming the 4-carbon OAA — the first stable product of C4.

questions.question: Photorespiration is wasteful because it
options: consumes ATP and releases CO2 without producing sugar
questions.explanation: At high O2 and low CO2, RuBisCO fixes O2 instead, producing one 3-C and one 2-C compound, releasing CO2 with no sugar — C3 plants lose up to 25% of fixed carbon.

questions.question: In C4 plants, RuBisCO is confined to
questions.explanation: PEP carboxylase works in mesophyll cells and RuBisCO in bundle sheath cells — spatial separation (kranz anatomy) is what prevents photorespiration.

questions.question: Blackman's law of limiting factors states that the rate of photosynthesis is limited by
questions.explanation: While CO2 is the major limiting factor in nature, any factor (light, CO2, water, temperature) can limit the rate when it is deficient.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Photosynthesis in Higher Plants

questions.question: Cyclic photophosphorylation produces
questions.explanation: Only PS I is involved and the electron returns to PS I; no water splitting occurs, hence no NADPH and no O2 — it happens in stroma lamellae.

questions.question: Chemiosmotic hypothesis of ATP synthesis in chloroplasts was proposed by
questions.explanation: Protons accumulate inside the thylakoid lumen; ATP synthase (CF0-CF1) uses the proton gradient to make ATP from ADP and Pi.

questions.question: Which of the following is TRUE for chlorophyll a?
options: It absorbs maximally in the blue and red regions
It is present only in C4 plants
questions.explanation: Chlorophyll a shows absorption peaks near 430 nm (blue) and 660 nm (red); green light is reflected — which is why leaves look green.

questions.question: To fix six molecules of CO2 into one glucose molecule in the Calvin cycle, the requirement is
questions.explanation: Per CO2 the cost is 3 ATP + 2 NADPH; six turns of the Calvin cycle need 18 ATP and 12 NADPH to make one glucose.

questions.question: Which experiment used a prism to split light and demonstrated that maximum photosynthesis occurs in blue and red light?
questions.explanation: Engelmann used a prism with the alga Cladophora and aerobic bacteria, which accumulated in the blue and red regions — the action spectrum.

questions.question: C4 plants are more productive than C3 plants at high temperature because
options: they have no photorespiration and their PEP carboxylase has high CO2 affinity
questions.explanation: At high temperature stomata close, internal CO2 falls and C3 plants lose carbon by photorespiration; the C4 mechanism concentrates CO2 in bundle sheath cells, avoiding the loss.

practiceSets.name: 🩺 NEET Drill — Respiration in Plants

questions.question: Glycolysis occurs in
questions.explanation: Glycolysis is the common pathway of all respiration and needs no oxygen. Net gain: 2 ATP, 2 NADH and 2 pyruvate per glucose.

questions.question: The net ATP gain in glycolysis is
questions.explanation: Four ATP are produced by substrate-level phosphorylation and two are spent in the preparatory phase, leaving a net of 2 ATP plus 2 NADH.

questions.question: The rate-limiting enzyme of glycolysis is
questions.explanation: PFK (phosphofructokinase) catalyses the committed step converting fructose-6-phosphate to fructose-1,6-bisphosphate.

questions.question: Pyruvate is converted to acetyl CoA by
options: oxidative decarboxylation in the mitochondrial matrix
questions.explanation: Pyruvate dehydrogenase removes CO2 and produces NADH; the 2-carbon acetyl CoA then enters the Krebs cycle.

questions.question: The Krebs cycle occurs in
questions.explanation: Also called the TCA cycle, it is the second stage after glycolysis; per turn it yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH2, 1 GTP/ATP and 2 CO2.

questions.question: The respiratory quotient (RQ) of fats is
questions.explanation: Fats are poor in oxygen and consume more O2 per CO2 released, so RQ = CO2/O2 < 1. Carbohydrates give RQ = 1, while organic acids (e.g. malic acid) exceed 1.

questions.question: In the ETS, oxygen acts as
questions.explanation: Oxygen accepts electrons at complex IV and combines with protons to form water. Water is thus the end product of the ETS, not a reactant.

questions.question: Anaerobic respiration in yeast produces
questions.explanation: Alcoholic fermentation: pyruvate → ethanol + CO2 with only 2 ATP per glucose. Muscle cells produce lactic acid from pyruvate with no CO2.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Respiration in Plants

questions.question: The net ATP gain per molecule of glucose in aerobic respiration (NCERT) is
questions.explanation: NCERT computes 38 ATP in total (10 NADH × 3 + 2 FADH2 × 2 + 4 by substrate-level phosphorylation), but the net gain is 36 ATP because the two cytoplasmic NADH from glycolysis are shuttled into the mitochondrion.

questions.question: Oxidative phosphorylation occurs in
questions.explanation: The ETS is coupled to ATP synthesis across the inner membrane — the chemiosmotic mechanism of Peter Mitchell, with protons pumped into the intermembrane space.

questions.question: Which steps of the Krebs cycle release CO2?
options: Formation of citrate from oxaloacetate and acetyl CoA
Conversion of isocitrate to α-ketoglutarate and of α-ketoglutarate to succinyl CoA
questions.explanation: Two oxidative decarboxylations release 2 CO2 per turn of the cycle — the carbon in the exhaled CO2 of plants and animals ultimately comes from here.

questions.question: The number of NADH molecules produced per glucose in the Krebs cycle is
questions.explanation: Per glucose: 2 turns of the cycle × 3 NADH = 6 NADH, plus 2 FADH2. Glycolysis adds 2 more NADH (total 8 NADH equivalents).

questions.question: Respiration is called amphibolic because
options: it both breaks down and builds up organic molecules (catabolic and anabolic intermediates)
it occurs in both plants and animals
both aerobic and anaerobic forms exist
water is both used and produced
questions.explanation: Krebs cycle intermediates (e.g. α-ketoglutarate, OAA) are used to synthesise amino acids and fatty acids — the reason respiration is not purely catabolic.

questions.question: By the end of the electron transport chain, water is formed by
options: the reaction of protons with oxygen after electron acceptance
questions.explanation: Complexes I, III and IV pump protons; oxygen accepts electrons and combines with 2H+ at the end — 2H+ + ½O2 + 2e− → H2O.

questions.question: Apical dominance is caused by
options: auxin produced by the apical bud
questions.explanation: Auxin from the apex suppresses the growth of lateral buds; removing the apex (decapitation) releases them — this is why pruning makes a plant bushy.

questions.question: The hormone that promotes internode elongation and causes 'bolting' is
questions.explanation: GA3 sprayed on sugarcane increases cane length; in cabbage a rosette plant bolts (stem elongates) under gibberellins.

questions.question: Cell division is promoted mainly by
questions.explanation: Cytokinins are synthesised in regions of rapid cell division (root tips, developing fruits) and also delay leaf senescence (Richmond-Lang effect).

questions.question: Abscisic acid is called the stress hormone because it
options: closes stomata and induces seed dormancy
questions.explanation: ABA increases under drought and salinity stress, closing stomata to reduce water loss and inhibiting growth — the antagonist of gibberellin.

questions.question: The hormone responsible for fruit ripening is
questions.explanation: Ethylene is a gaseous PGR that also breaks dormancy, promotes senescence and causes epinasty — used commercially to ripen bananas and mangoes.

questions.question: The phenomenon in which a plant's flowering depends on the relative length of day and night is
questions.explanation: Photoperiodism is perceived by the LEAVES (not the bud), and the floral stimulus then travels to the shoot apex to induce flowering.

questions.question: A plant that flowers only when the dark period exceeds a critical duration is a
questions.explanation: Actually SDPs need a long CONTINUOUS dark period; interrupting the night with a flash of light prevents flowering — a classic experimental question.

questions.question: Vernalisation is
options: the promotion of flowering by long days
the inhibition of growth by cold
the ripening of fruits by ethylene
the promotion of flowering by a period of low temperature
questions.explanation: Winter varieties of wheat and barley need cold treatment. The effect can also be replaced by gibberellins — the classic experiment in this chapter.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Plant Growth and Development

questions.question: The growth rate is called arithmetic when
options: only one daughter cell continues to divide while the other differentiates
questions.explanation: Arithmetic growth (linear curve) is typical of root elongation; geometrical growth (sigmoid curve with lag, log and stationary phases) suits cells that double.

questions.question: 2,4-D is used as a
options: herbicide to kill dicot weeds in a cereal field
questions.explanation: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin: broad-leaved dicots are killed while monocot cereals survive — selective weedicide.

questions.question: Which of the following is antagonistic to gibberellin in seed germination?
questions.explanation: GA breaks dormancy and promotes germination; ABA induces and maintains dormancy. Their balance decides whether a seed stays dormant.

questions.question: Richmond-Lang effect refers to
options: delay of leaf senescence by cytokinin
questions.explanation: Cytokinins delay the ageing of leaves by mobilising nutrients to the treated region — the reason cytokinins are called 'anti-ageing' hormones.

questions.question: The PGR used to induce parthenocarpy in tomatoes is
questions.explanation: Auxin treatment produces seedless fruits. Gibberellins also induce parthenocarpy in some fruits; ethylene promotes senescence instead.

questions.question: For most plants, the photoperiodic stimulus is perceived by
questions.explanation: The leaf perceives the light/dark cycle and produces a florigen-like stimulus that migrates to the shoot apex — proven by grafting experiments.

questions.question: Tidal volume of a healthy human is about
questions.explanation: TV ≈ 500 mL per breath. Inspiratory reserve volume ≈ 2500–3000 mL, expiratory reserve volume ≈ 1000–1100 mL, residual volume ≈ 1100–1200 mL.

questions.question: Vital capacity is
options: the maximum volume of air a person can exhale after a maximum inspiration
the air remaining after a forced expiration
total lung capacity minus tidal volume
questions.explanation: VC = TV + IRV + ERV ≈ 3500–4500 mL. Residual air cannot be expelled (1100 mL), which is why lungs never collapse.

questions.question: Oxygen is transported in blood mainly as
questions.explanation: 97% as oxyhaemoglobin and 3% dissolved in plasma. Each Hb can bind four O2 molecules at its iron centres.

questions.question: Carbon dioxide is transported mainly as
questions.explanation: 70% as bicarbonate, 20–25% as carbamino-haemoglobin and 7% dissolved in plasma. Carbonic anhydrase in RBCs speeds up the conversion.

questions.question: The oxygen dissociation curve is
options: sigmoid, shifting right with low pH, high CO2 and high temperature
a straight line passing through the origin
questions.explanation: A right shift means less affinity for O2 and more unloading at tissues — that is the Bohr effect, essential for O2 delivery to active muscles.

questions.question: The respiratory rhythm centre is located in
questions.explanation: The medulla has the rhythm centre, the pons has the pneumotaxic centre that moderates it, and chemosensitive areas respond to CO2 and H+.

questions.question: Emphysema is characterised by
options: damage to the alveolar walls, reducing the surface area for gas exchange
questions.explanation: Chronic smoking causes emphysema; asthma is the allergic condition of the bronchi, and bronchitis is inflammation of the bronchi with mucus.

questions.question: During inspiration
options: the ribs move downward and inward
the diaphragm contracts and the volume of the thoracic cavity increases
questions.explanation: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals increases volume, lowering intrapulmonary pressure below atmospheric so air rushes in.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Breathing and Exchange of Gases

questions.question: The diffusion membrane of the alveoli is made of
options: three layers: alveolar squamous epithelium, basement substance and capillary endothelium
questions.explanation: Its total thickness is less than a millimetre — the reason gas exchange is so rapid despite a huge alveolar surface area (~80 m²).

questions.question: Which of the following volumes cannot be measured by a spirometer?
questions.explanation: A spirometer measures air moved in and out; residual volume always remains in the lungs and needs indirect methods (e.g. helium dilution).

questions.question: The chloride shift refers to
options: the movement of chloride into plasma
the movement of chloride ions into RBCs to maintain electrical neutrality during CO2 transport
questions.explanation: As bicarbonate leaves the RBC, chloride enters to balance the charge — a small detail that appears in assertion-reason questions.

questions.question: Which of the following has the highest affinity for oxygen?
options: Haemoglobin in the alveoli (high pO2, low pCO2)
questions.explanation: In the alveoli the conditions favour binding; in the tissues, high pCO2, low pH and high temperature favour release — this gradient drives gas exchange.

questions.question: Carbonic anhydrase is present in
questions.explanation: The enzyme inside RBCs catalyses CO2 + H2O ⇌ H2CO3, greatly speeding up CO2 transport as bicarbonate.

questions.question: Inspiratory capacity equals
questions.explanation: IC = TV + IRV (~3500 mL); functional residual capacity = ERV + RV (~2500 mL). Draw a simple cylinder diagram with all volumes and this is settled.

questions.question: The percentage of plasma in blood is about
questions.explanation: Plasma ≈ 55% and formed elements ≈ 45%. Plasma is 90–92% water, with proteins (albumin, globulin, fibrinogen) making up most of the rest.

questions.question: Which plasma protein is most abundant and helps maintain osmotic balance?
questions.explanation: Albumins are the most abundant plasma proteins; globulins defend against infection and fibrinogen is needed for clotting.

questions.question: The most abundant type of WBC in human blood is
questions.explanation: Neutrophils are the most numerous (60–65%) and phogocytic; lymphocytes (20–25%) are next; basophils are the rarest (0.5–1%).

questions.question: Eosinophils are associated with
questions.explanation: Neutrophils and monocytes are phagocytic, basophils release histamine and heparin, and eosinophils handle allergy and parasitic infections.

questions.question: The pacemaker of the human heart is
questions.explanation: The SA node in the right atrium generates the impulse (~70–75 per minute) — the human heart is myogenic, so it beats without nerve input.

questions.question: The QRS complex of an ECG represents
questions.explanation: P = atrial depolarisation (contraction), QRS = ventricular depolarisation, T = ventricular repolarisation. Counting QRS complexes gives the heart rate.

questions.question: Cardiac output of a healthy adult is about
questions.explanation: Cardiac output = stroke volume (≈70 mL) × heart rate (≈72/min) ≈ 5000 mL. It can rise to 20–25 L/min during heavy exercise.

questions.question: Erythroblastosis fetalis occurs when
options: an Rh-positive mother carries an Rh-negative foetus
the mother has blood group O only
an Rh-negative mother carries an Rh-positive foetus
questions.explanation: Maternal anti-Rh antibodies cross the placenta in a subsequent pregnancy and destroy foetal RBCs — prevented by anti-Rh (RhoGAM) injection after delivery.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Body Fluids and Circulation

questions.question: Which of the following is the universal donor blood group?
questions.explanation: O has no A or B antigens (safe for all recipients), and Rh-negative avoids sensitisation. AB positive is the universal recipient.

questions.question: Lymph differs from blood in that it
options: has no RBCs but has lymphocytes and is colourless
questions.explanation: Lymph is the interstitial fluid that enters lymph vessels; it carries lymphocytes and helps in immunity and fat absorption.

questions.question: The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle is
questions.explanation: Right = tricuspid, left = bicuspid (mitral). The three cusps on the right, two on the left — the atrioventricular valves prevent backflow into the atria.

questions.question: During the cardiac cycle, which of the following is the duration of one cycle?
questions.explanation: 0.8 s = atrial systole (0.1) + ventricular systole (0.3) + joint diastole (0.4). At 72 beats per minute this is exactly 60/72 s.

questions.question: Which of the following statements about the human heart is correct?
options: It is myogenic and four-chambered with the left ventricle having the thickest wall
The right ventricle has the thickest wall
questions.explanation: The left ventricle pumps blood to the whole body, so it works hardest and has the thickest muscular wall.

questions.question: Double circulation means
options: blood circulates in two opposite directions
blood passes twice through the heart in one complete circuit
blood flow through arteries and veins only
questions.explanation: Pulmonary circulation (right side) and systemic circulation (left side) are separate — this keeps oxygenated and deoxygenated blood from mixing, essential for warm-blooded animals.

questions.question: Bony fishes are
questions.explanation: Aquatic animals excrete ammonia (highly soluble, needs plenty of water). Cartilaginous fishes and mammals are ureotelic; birds, reptiles and insects are uricotelic.

questions.question: The functional unit of the kidney is
questions.explanation: Each human kidney has about 1 million nephrons, each with a malpighian corpuscle (glomerulus + Bowman's capsule) and a renal tubule.

questions.question: Glomerular filtration rate in a healthy person is about
questions.explanation: GFR ≈ 125 mL/min ≈ 180 litres per day; about 99% is reabsorbed, so urine output is only 1–1.5 litres a day.

questions.question: Maximum reabsorption occurs in the
questions.explanation: The PCT reabsorbs nearly all essential nutrients, 70–80% of electrolytes and water — it is the workhorse of the nephron.

questions.question: Which part of the nephron is impermeable to water?
options: Ascending limb of the loop of Henle
Descending limb of the loop of Henle
questions.explanation: The descending limb is permeable to water but not solutes; the ascending limb is impermeable to water but transports electrolytes — the basis of the counter current mechanism.

questions.question: Antidiuretic hormone (ADH) acts on the
options: DCT and collecting duct to increase water reabsorption
questions.explanation: ADH from the posterior pituitary increases water reabsorption, reducing urine volume; alcohol inhibits ADH, which is why it increases urine output.

questions.question: The enzyme renin is released by
options: juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole
questions.explanation: Renin starts the renin-angiotensin mechanism, which raises blood pressure and stimulates aldosterone release for Na+ and water reabsorption.

questions.question: The micturition reflex is triggered by
options: stretching of the urinary bladder wall
questions.explanation: Stretch receptors send signals to the CNS; the sphincter relaxes and urine is expelled. Adults can voluntarily control this reflex.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Excretory Products and their Elimination

questions.question: Uric acid is the main nitrogenous waste in
questions.explanation: Uricotelic animals excrete uric acid as pellets or paste — an adaptation to conserve water, at the cost of spending energy to synthesise it.

questions.question: The counter current mechanism involves
options: the loop of Henle and the vasa recta maintaining a concentration gradient in the medulla
Bowman's capsule and the collecting duct
questions.explanation: Flow in opposite directions in the two limbs and in the vasa recta maintains a 300 → 1200 mOsm gradient, allowing urine to be concentrated up to four times the plasma.

questions.question: Which of the following increases sodium reabsorption in the DCT?
questions.explanation: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex promotes Na+ and water reabsorption and K+ secretion. ANF from the heart does the opposite, causing vasodilation.

questions.question: The collecting duct releases urea into the interstitium to
options: maintain the osmolarity of the medullary interstitium
questions.explanation: Urea recycling adds to the medullary gradient — a subtle but often-asked NCERT point about concentrating urine.

questions.question: An artificial kidney works on the principle of
options: dialysis using a selectively permeable membrane
questions.explanation: In haemodialysis, blood is passed through cellophane tubes bathed in dialysing fluid; wastes diffuse out while plasma proteins and cells stay inside.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a function of the kidney?
questions.explanation: Erythropoietin stimulates RBC formation, but the kidney only SECRETES it; RBCs are actually formed in bone marrow. The kidney regulates BP, electrolytes, pH and wastes.

questions.question: The functional unit of a myofibril is
options: the sarcomere (the region between two successive Z lines)
questions.explanation: A sarcomere contains the A band (dark, myosin) and the I band (light, actin). Contraction shortens the sarcomere length.

questions.question: During muscle contraction
options: the A band remains the same while the I band shortens
the I band remains the same
questions.explanation: Sliding filament theory: thin actin filaments slide over thick myosin, so the I band (actin-rich) reduces and the H zone narrows, while the A band (myosin) stays constant.

questions.question: Calcium ions released during muscle contraction bind to
questions.explanation: Ca²⁺ binds troponin, exposing the myosin-binding sites on actin; then cross-bridges form and the filaments slide — the signal for contraction.

questions.question: Which of the following joints is immovable?
questions.explanation: Fibrous joints (sutures) are immovable, cartilaginous joints are partially movable and synovial joints are freely movable.

questions.question: The joint between the atlas and the occipital condyles is a
questions.explanation: Knuckle-like joint types: hinge = knee/elbow, ball and socket = shoulder/hip, pivot = atlas-axis, gliding = tarsals, saddle = thumb carpals.

questions.question: Myasthenia gravis is caused by
options: an autoimmune attack on the neuromuscular junction
questions.explanation: Antibodies block acetylcholine receptors, causing fatigue and muscle weakness. Gout is due to uric acid accumulation in joints.

questions.question: Red muscle fibres differ from white fibres in having
options: numerous mitochondria and myoglobin with slow sustained contraction
questions.explanation: Red fibres are aerobic and fatigue-resistant; white fibres rely on anaerobic glycolysis and fatigue quickly — the classic endurance vs sprint distinction.

questions.question: Osteoporosis is characterised by
options: decreased bone mass due to reduced oestrogen, common after menopause
questions.explanation: Age-related loss of bone mineral density makes bones brittle — calcium, vitamin D and exercise help delay it.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Locomotion and Movement

questions.question: The number of bones in the human skull is
questions.explanation: Skull = 22 (8 cranial + 14 facial). The vertebral column has 26 vertebrae, ribs 12 pairs, hyoid 1 — the axial skeleton totals 80 bones.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT part of the axial skeleton?
questions.explanation: The appendicular skeleton is made of the pectoral and pelvic girdles and the limb bones — 126 bones; the axial skeleton has 80.

questions.question: ATP for muscle contraction is provided by
options: creatine phosphate in the initial phase and by aerobic/anaerobic respiration later
questions.explanation: Muscles use ATP and creatine phosphate as immediate reserves, then switch to glycolysis and oxidative phosphorylation as the effort continues.

questions.question: Gout is caused by the deposition of
questions.explanation: Inflammation of the joints due to excess uric acid crystals — associated with purine-rich diets and impaired excretion.

questions.question: Which muscle type is found in the wall of the heart?
options: Cardiac muscle — involuntary and striated with intercalated discs
questions.explanation: Cardiac muscle cells are branched and joined by intercalated discs that allow the impulse to spread, making the heart contract as a unit.

questions.question: The sliding filament theory was proposed by
questions.explanation: The Huxley model explains contraction as the sliding of actin filaments over myosin filaments — no filament changes length.

questions.question: The resting membrane potential of a neuron is about
questions.explanation: Maintained by the Na⁺-K⁺ ATPase (3 Na⁺ out, 2 K⁺ in) and differential permeability — the neuron is polarised at rest.

questions.question: Depolarisation of the axon membrane is due to
questions.explanation: Na⁺ channels open, Na⁺ rushes in and the membrane becomes positive inside; repolarisation then follows by K⁺ efflux.

questions.question: The impulse jumps from node to node in a myelinated fibre. This is called
questions.explanation: Myelin is insulating, so depolarisation occurs only at the nodes of Ranvier — making conduction much faster and less energy-consuming.

questions.question: Which part of the brain maintains posture and balance?
questions.explanation: The cerebellum coordinates body movements and balance; the medulla controls respiration and cardiovascular reflexes; the cerebrum is the seat of intelligence and memory.

questions.question: The reflex arc consists of
options: receptor → sensory neuron → CNS → motor neuron → effector
questions.explanation: Reflex action is a quick involuntary response; the spinal cord is often the integrating centre, allowing the brain to be informed afterwards.

questions.question: Rods of the retina contain
options: rhodopsin and function in dim light
questions.explanation: Rods dominate in twilight vision, cones respond to bright light and colour. The fovea has only cones; the optic disc (blind spot) has neither.

questions.question: The part of the ear that contains the organ of hearing is
questions.explanation: The cochlea's organ of Corti has hair cells that transduce sound; the semicircular canals and utricle/saccule are for balance and equilibrium.

questions.question: The autonomic nervous system is divided into
questions.explanation: Sympathetic prepares the body for emergencies (fight or flight), parasympathetic restores calm — they are antagonistic and both use the same organs.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Neural Control and Coordination

questions.question: Myelinated nerve fibres are enveloped by
questions.explanation: In the peripheral nervous system, Schwann cells wrap the axon to form the myelin sheath; gaps between them are the nodes of Ranvier.

questions.question: Which part of the brain acts as the major coordination centre for sensory and motor signalling?
questions.explanation: The thalamus is the relay centre for sensory and motor impulses; the hypothalamus controls temperature, hunger, thirst and hormone release.

questions.question: Chemical synapses transmit the impulse through
options: neurotransmitters such as acetylcholine across the synaptic cleft
questions.explanation: In a chemical synapse, the impulse causes release of neurotransmitters that bind receptors on the postsynaptic membrane — the basis of association, learning and memory.

questions.question: The cerebrospinal fluid is found in
options: the ventricles of the brain and the central canal of the spinal cord
questions.explanation: CSF is a clear, colourless fluid that protects the brain, provides buoyancy and is formed by the choroid plexus; its flow brings nutrition and removes wastes.

questions.question: Which of the following is part of the limbic system?
questions.explanation: The limbic system (with the hypothalamus and amygdala) controls emotions, motivation and memory — often called the 'emotional brain'.

questions.question: Na⁺-K⁺ pump in a nerve cell transports
options: 3 Na⁺ out and 2 K⁺ in per ATP
questions.explanation: The 3:2 ratio makes the inside more negative — the origin of the resting potential and the reason it costs ATP.

questions.question: Which of the following is a steroid hormone?
questions.explanation: Steroids (cortisol, aldosterone, testosterone, oestrogen, progesterone) act on intracellular receptors; peptide hormones (insulin, glucagon, ADH) use membrane receptors and second messengers like cAMP.

questions.question: ADH and oxytocin are secreted by the
questions.explanation: They are synthesised in the hypothalamus and released from the posterior pituitary — the classic neurosecretion pathway.

questions.question: Excess growth hormone in an adult causes
questions.explanation: In children excess GH causes gigantism, deficiency causes pituitary dwarfism; in adults the long bones cannot grow, so the jaw, hands and feet enlarge — acromegaly.

questions.question: The hormone secreted by the thyroid that lowers blood calcium is
questions.explanation: Thyrocalcitonin (TCT) lowers serum Ca²⁺ by promoting its deposition in bone; parathormone (PTH) raises it — they are antagonistic partners.

questions.question: Graves' disease (exophthalmic goitre) is caused by
questions.explanation: Symptoms: enlarged thyroid, bulging eyes (exophthalmos), increased metabolic rate and weight loss. Iodine deficiency causes simple goitre/hypothyroidism.

questions.question: Addison's disease results from
questions.explanation: Deficiency of cortisol and aldosterone causes weakness, bronzing of skin and low blood pressure. Cushing's syndrome is the opposite (excess cortisol).

questions.question: Insulin is secreted by the
options: β cells of the islets of Langerhans
questions.explanation: β cells secrete insulin (lowers blood glucose), α cells glucagon (raises it) and δ cells somatostatin — a three-way control system.

questions.question: Melatonin, which regulates the sleep-wake cycle, is secreted by the
questions.explanation: Melatonin also influences the reproductive cycle and pigmentation. The thymus, by contrast, secretes thymosins for T-cell development.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Chemical Coordination and Integration

questions.question: Which hormone stimulates the reabsorption of water in the kidney tubules?
questions.explanation: ADH deficiency causes diabetes insipidus — passing large volumes of dilute urine. Aldosterone acts on Na⁺, not directly on water alone.

questions.question: Cretinism in children is due to
options: hypothyroidism with mental retardation and stunted growth
questions.explanation: Congenital hypothyroidism causes cretinism; the adult form is myxoedema. Iodised salt prevents these disorders.

questions.question: Which hormone is responsible for the fight-or-flight response?
questions.explanation: Adrenaline and noradrenaline increase heart rate, blood glucose and blood flow to skeletal muscles — emergency hormones secreted under stress.

questions.question: Relaxin is secreted by the
options: the ovary (corpus luteum) in the later phase of pregnancy
questions.explanation: NCERT: relaxin is secreted by the ovary in the later phase of pregnancy; it relaxes the pelvic ligaments and widens the cervix for delivery.

questions.question: Which one is NOT a hypothalamic releasing hormone?
questions.explanation: The hypothalamus releases TRH, CRH, GnRH, GHRH and others that control the anterior pituitary; thyroxine is the hormone made by the thyroid itself.

questions.question: Somatostatin from the pancreas
options: inhibits the secretion of glucagon and insulin
questions.explanation: Somatostatin (also from the hypothalamus) is an inhibitory hormone — a fine example of negative feedback within the islets.

questions.question: The layer of the microsporangium that nourishes the developing pollen grains is
questions.explanation: The tapetum is the innermost of the four wall layers and provides nourishment; its cells often become polyploid and secrete sporopollenin.

questions.question: The mature pollen grain of most angiosperms is
options: 2-celled with a vegetative cell and a generative cell
questions.explanation: The generative cell divides to give two male gametes inside the pollen tube. About 60% of angiosperms shed 2-celled pollen; the rest are 3-celled.

questions.question: The embryo sac of a typical angiosperm is
questions.explanation: Three antipodals, two synergids, one egg and one central cell with two polar nuclei = 7 cells, 8 nuclei. The synergids bear the filiform apparatus.

questions.question: Megaspore mother cell undergoes meiosis to produce
options: four megaspores, of which only one remains functional
questions.explanation: Monosporic development: three megaspores degenerate and the functional one undergoes three mitotic divisions to form the 8-nucleate embryo sac.

questions.question: Double fertilisation involves
options: syngamy and triple fusion in the same embryo sac
fusion of two male gametes with two eggs
questions.explanation: One male gamete fuses with the egg (2n zygote) and the other with the two polar nuclei (3n PEN) — a unique feature of angiosperms.

questions.question: The ploidy of the endosperm in angiosperms is
questions.explanation: The PEN (primary endosperm nucleus) is 3n and forms the endosperm; in gymnosperms the endosperm is haploid and formed before fertilisation.

questions.question: Apomixis is
options: the production of fruits without seeds
the production of seeds without fertilisation
questions.explanation: Apomixis produces clones of the parent — useful in hybrid seed production because hybrid characters are retained generation after generation.

questions.question: Which of the following is a chasmogamous flower?
options: A closed flower that never opens
One that is exposed with normal open petals
questions.explanation: Chasmogamous flowers are open, exposing anthers and stigma; cleistogamous flowers (Commelina, Oxalis) never open, ensuring autogamy.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants

questions.question: Geitonogamy is
options: pollination between two flowers of the same plant
questions.explanation: Geitonogamy is functionally cross-pollination (the pollen comes from a different flower) but genetically autogamy, since the plant is the same.

questions.question: Which of the following is pollinated by water?
questions.explanation: Hydrophily occurs in Zostera and Vallisneria (examples: Vallisneria's ribbon-like pollen). Salvia and Ficus use insects; Yucca has a mutualistic moth.

questions.question: The pollen tube enters the ovule through the micropyle. This is called
questions.explanation: Entry through the micropyle = porogamy (most common); through the chalaza = chalazogamy; through the integuments = mesogamy.

questions.question: Which structure develops into the seed coat?
questions.explanation: After fertilisation, the ovule becomes the seed: integuments → seed coat, nucellus → perisperm (if retained), zygote → embryo, PEN → endosperm.

questions.question: False fruit is one where the
options: thalamus contributes to the fruit, as in apple
ovary wall is the edible part
questions.explanation: Apple and cashew are false fruits (thalamus/peduncle contributes); mango and coconut are true fruits since the ovary becomes the fruit.

questions.question: Polyembryony in citrus is due to
questions.explanation: Adventive polyembryony: nucellar cells divide and form embryos, so a seed can contain several seedlings genetically identical to the mother.

questions.question: Sertoli cells in the seminiferous tubules
questions.explanation: Sertoli (nurse) cells provide nutrition; Leydig (interstitial) cells secrete androgens such as testosterone.

questions.question: The scrotum keeps the testes at a temperature
options: 2–2.5 °C lower than the body, needed for spermatogenesis
questions.explanation: Spermatogenesis needs a lower temperature; the scrotum's position outside the body maintains the 2–2.5 °C difference.

questions.question: Acrosome of a sperm contains
options: hydrolytic enzymes that help in penetration of the egg
questions.explanation: Acrosome (from the Golgi) caps the head; the middle piece packed with mitochondria supplies energy and the tail gives motility.

questions.question: Primary oocyte is arrested at which stage until puberty?
questions.explanation: It is arrested in prophase I inside the primary follicle. It completes meiosis I just before ovulation, and the secondary oocyte is arrested at metaphase II until fertilisation.

questions.question: Ovulation in a 28-day cycle occurs around day
questions.explanation: The LH surge on about day 14 ruptures the Graafian follicle and releases the secondary oocyte; the luteal phase then follows.

questions.question: The corpus luteum secretes
options: oestrogen only in the follicular phase
questions.explanation: Progesterone from the corpus luteum supports pregnancy in the early stages; if fertilisation does not occur, it degenerates and menstruation begins.

questions.question: Fertilisation in humans normally occurs in the
options: ampullary-isthmic junction of the fallopian tube
questions.explanation: The sperm and ovum fuse at the ampullary-isthmic junction; the zygote then divides while travelling down to the uterus for implantation.

questions.question: Colostrum is rich in
options: antibodies that give the newborn passive immunity
questions.explanation: The yellowish first milk contains IgA antibodies, essential for the infant's immune protection in the first days after birth.

practiceSets.name: 🎯 PYQ Drill — Human Reproduction

questions.question: Which hormone surge triggers ovulation?
questions.explanation: The mid-cycle LH surge ruptures the follicle. FSH dominates the follicular phase, progesterone the luteal phase.

questions.question: The two components of the blastocyst are
questions.explanation: The trophoblast attaches to the endometrium for implantation (later forming the placenta); the inner cell mass becomes the embryo.

questions.question: Implantation of the blastocyst occurs in the
questions.explanation: Attachment and embedding in the endometrium takes about a week after fertilisation, at the blastocyst stage.

questions.question: hCG, hPL and progesterone during pregnancy are secreted by the
options: placenta (hCG initially also by the trophoblast)
questions.explanation: hCG maintains the corpus luteum in early pregnancy; the placenta later takes over hormone production entirely.

questions.question: Oxytocin at parturition causes
options: strong uterine contractions for the foetal ejection reflex
questions.explanation: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary acts on the uterine muscle; relaxin from the placenta softens the pelvic ligaments.

questions.question: Spermiation is
options: the release of sperm from the epididymis
the release of sperms from the Sertoli cells into the lumen of the seminiferous tubules
questions.explanation: After spermiation the sperm pass through the rete testis, vasa efferentia, epididymis, vas deferens, ejaculatory duct and urethra.
